8. Operational Amplifiers (Opamp)

Opamp is the most widely applied integrated circuit.

8.1 Telescopic Opamp Topologies

An opamp amplifies a differential signal to a single-ended or a differential signal. The most fundamental topologies are OTA for single-ended and basic differential pair for differential output.

Basic Opamp Topologies

But the simple structures suffer from low gain. Suppose the OTA (a) is connected as a follower. The small-signal, low-frequency gain of both circuits is equal to . However, in nanometer technologies the intrinsic gain can hardly exceed 10. To alleviate this issue, the cascode topologies can be used, also called telescopic opamp.

Telescopic Topologies

Obviously such circuits display a gain of , but at the cost of output swing due to more devices in one path and additional poles due to extra parasitic capacitance.

For the single-ended output, the maximum output is limited to , while the minima is equal to . In low voltage applications, the effective range becomes extremely narrow. The differential output benifits from the virtue of differential pair and hence has a doubled swing .

Another drawback is the difficulty to configure a follower, i.e., connecting the output to the negative input.

8.2 Folded-Cascode Opamp

In order to alleviate the limited swing and difficulty to configure a follower, a folded-cascode opamp can be used. Recall the single-ended folded-cascode topology. The output swing changes from to . It looks that the swing doesn’t change too much. But is related to , hence the output swing of a not-folded-cascode is strongly limited by the input, while the folded-cascode is not. Hence, the folded-cascode decouples the input and output to provide a wider output swing.

Folded-cascode topology

However, since a folded-cascode requires two paths, it consumes more power.

Utilizing this topology, a telescopic opamp upgrades into a folded-cascode opamp.

Folded-cascode opamp

Under DC working point, the current should satisfy and . This relationship should be stablized by common-mode feedback which will be mentioned later to prevent deviation caused by the process and temperature drift.

8.3 Two-stage Opamp

In nanometer technologies the intrinsic gain of a MOS device can hardly exceed 10, hence the total gain of the one-stage opamps may fail to satisfy the requirement of “high gain” for opamps. Hence we may need a second stage to provide extra gain. But what’s the cost? Obviously, the power consumption.

Here is an example for two-stage opamp. The first stage is a telescopic opamp. For higher gain, this stage incorporates cascode devices. The second stage is configured as a CS stage. The overall voltage gain can be expressed as

Example for two-stage opamp

To configure a single-ended output, just connect one of the CS in the second stage as a current mirror. Note that the first stage maintains the differential output to suppress common-mode disturbance.

8.5 Common-mode Feedback (CMFB)

High-gain differential amplifier requires common-mode feedback (CMFB) because mismatch will severely affect the output common-mode level due to the large output imepdance. Take an example of basic differential pair, with loads of PMOS source and tail current .

Basic differential pair

Then the output CM level depends on how close and are to . Mismatch will drive the drain currents away from the equilibrium value, introducing finite differential-mode error. However, this small error will be amplified by the large output resistance to the output. We suppose the p-type source displays and , while n-type and . We wish them to match perfectly but impossible. At the output node, the mismatch current will produce a voltage of . Hence, we need common-mode feedback to eliminate the error of mismatch.

Sensing the CM level

The basic idea is to sense the common-mode output, compare with a reference voltage, and return it back to adjust the bias.

Common-mode feedback

First we need to solve “sensing”. Recall that . To construct a linear combination of voltages, just connect two resistors in series and you will get

Just set you will get the common-mode voltage at this node.

Common-mode feedback with resistors

The issue is that connecting a resistor at the output node will lower the output resistance. Hence this resistor should be chosen as greater as possible. But the most reliable method is to insert a source follower, but of course, consumes more power.

Common-mode feedback with resistors and SF

Note that and should be large enough or M7 and M8 will not be able to obtain adequate current when a large differential signal comes. Denote . Then

When a large differential swing comes, increase, if the resistors or the n-type current source are not large enough, will drop to 0 and M7 or M8 will be “starved”.

Inserting a SF will suffer from limitation of output swing. Without the SFs, ; with the SFs, . Thus the output swing is reduced approximately one . In low voltage applications this limitation cannot be neglected.

Another type of feedback is that utilizing a MOS in deep triode region as a resistor.

CMFB with MOS serving as resistors

It exhibits resistance at node P

The resistance depends on the common-mode only while independent on differential-mode. The resistance can thus be regarded as a measurement of common-mode level.

The difficulty of this method is that how to gurantee the deep triode region. The voltage at node P must be small enough, indicating that the sensed output common-mode level cannot be too low.

Feedback

The sensed signal should be sent back and adjust the common-mode level. One method is to compare the real value with a reference, amplify the error and send back to the current source to change the output level. Both the n-type current source in the output stage and the tail current source in the differential pair are active.

CMFB on different source

Utilizing MOS in deep triode region can avoid inserting another amplifier and save power budget.

8.6 Input Range Limitations

Consider a unity-gain buffer (follower), whose input range is nearly equal to the output range.

Folded-cascode unity-gain buffer

In this case the voltage swings are limited by the input differential pair rather than the output cascode branch.

Approximately one threshold larger than the cascode limitation .

A simple method is to apply complementary input stage. i.e., the input is sent to a PMOS pair and an NMOS pair simultaneously. When one pair is dead, the other works normally.

Complementary input stage

8.7 Gain-Bandwidth Product

For a given opamp under fixed bias, compensation, and load conditions, the gain-bandwidth product (GBW) is an approximately fixed small-signal specification. Negative feedback allows us to trade gain for bandwidth, but it does not increase this product. Recall that, for a single-pole amplifier, negative feedback moves the closed-loop pole farther from the origin by a factor of , where is the DC open-loop gain and is the feedback factor.

To see why the product is constant, consider an opamp with the single-pole open-loop transfer function

where , the open-loop pole is at , and the open-loop bandwidth is . Assume a frequency-independent negative-feedback factor , with the differential input given by . The closed-loop transfer function is then

Thus the low-frequency closed-loop gain and the closed-loop pole are

The pole moves to a higher frequency, increasing the bandwidth to

Feedback therefore reduces the gain and increases the bandwidth by exactly the same factor. Multiplying the two gives

The feedback factor cancels, so this product is independent of in the single-pole model. Gain here is a linear voltage ratio, rather than a value in decibels, and GBW is expressed in hertz. Because the opamp’s open-loop gain and pole frequency are fixed under the assumed operating conditions, reducing increases the closed-loop gain but moves the closed-loop pole back toward the open-loop pole, reducing the bandwidth. For ,

For example, an opamp with a GBW of provides approximately of bandwidth at a closed-loop gain of 10, or at a gain of 100, provided the single-pole approximation remains valid.

GBW is also approximately equal to the open-loop unity-gain frequency . Setting gives

where the approximation requires . In a real opamp, the constant-product rule applies over the range dominated by a single pole; additional poles and changes in operating conditions can cause deviations. For an inverting configuration, the bandwidth is governed by the noise gain , rather than by the magnitude of the signal gain. This small-signal bandwidth limit is distinct from the large-signal slew-rate limit discussed next.

8.8 Slew Rate

Generally, if an ideal voltage signal passes through an RC lowpass network, suppose the voltage rises from to abruptly, the output voltage rises exponentially. The instant rising slope is equal to . However, if the voltage source has a finite maximum driving current , once exceeds the maximum value, the slope will become a ramp, instead of exponential. The ramp slope will be determined by the charging speed to the capacitor by the maximum current.

This maximum voltage rising slope is called slew rate. Generally, we say the bandwidth of small signals is determined by the gain-bandwidth product (GBW), while that of the large signals determined by slew rate.

Take the most simple opamp, 5-devices OTA for example.

Slew rate of OTA

When a large differential swing comes, suppose that of M1 rises abruptly and is large enough. Then M1 absorbs all of and M2 is starved. The p-type current mirror then copy all current in M1 path toward the output node. Since M2 has no current, all flows out, inside (assume is large enough). Then the slew rate is

When the input drops, the process is the same, at this time M1 is starved and M2 absorbs all the current. We can notice that when the output slope reaches a ramp, it becomes independent of the input.

For a differential-output telescopic opamp, obviously the slew rate is equal to because each p-type source provides .

Slew rate of telescopic opamp

Then we consider a single-output folded-cascode opamp. .

Slew rate of folded-cascode opamp

If , when M1 absorbs all , the n-type source experiences . After copying, the output current is still and no devices will be starved. The slew rate is equal to . In practice we choose .

However, if , M9 cannot provide enough current when M1 absorbs all under nominal condition. An is mandatorily drawn from M9. With the effect of CLM, increases severely, producing a considerably voltage drop at node X. Then M1 and enters triode region, decreasing the current, recovering the node voltage gradually.

Long recovery of node voltage

This drop and slow recovery will slow the device’s speed down. To alleviate this issue, we can add two clamp devices. When the opamp is working properly, and tend to be high. By designing M9 and M10 properly, M11 and M12 is turned off. When voltage at X drops, rises and M12 is turned on, providing an extra current (different between and ) to assist on recovery of the voltage. The figure (b) is a more aggressive operation. Since the source is usually higher than , M11 and M12 are off during small signal operations.
